""Hey there welcome to Dear Blco. Let's answer an audience question shall we? Scotty Charles asks "Dear Blanco why do some people love collecting stuff? My uncle has an entire room of unopened toys he calls important historical artifacts." Huh. Well great question. Whether it's action figures comic books Pokémon cards or that Laboo collection your cousin swears will make him rich one day collecting is everywhere. Studies show that around 30 to 40% of people in the US consider themselves collectors. And globally the hobby spans all cultures ages and income levels including some of the Lifenaggin team members. So why do people go this hard for collectibles? Well for many collecting taps into nostalgia that warm fuzzy feeling you get remembering your childhood. Think of it like emotional time travel. Instead of a time machine you've got an old Game Boy and a stack of comic books. Studies show that nostalgia can make you feel really good reinforce one's own identity and even reduce your stress levels. Is collecting nostalgic items being used to mask a deeper sadness with how things might be in your life currently? Ask yourself whether building your happiness entirely on how good things were in your childhood is truly sustainable or healthy. I am not diagnosing your uncle or anyone for that matter. Collecting is a very complicated hobby emotionally and physically. Then there's the adrenaline rush. Hunting down a rare item releases dopamine your brain's feel-good chemical. It's a scavenger hunt mixed with a lottery win. Especially if we're talking about the ultra rare Toxic Grig Fighter Series 3 glow-in-the-dark meltdown mode Greek with detachable toxic sludge hands. Triangle Bob just got one after taking out a second mortgage but according to him totally worth it. But just remember some people compare it to gambling. If you keep reinforcing that the area of your brain that tells you "Hey maybe we should cut our losses like the prefrontal cortex won't be as strong." Some collectors are completionists. They need every single item in a set all the variants limited editions and that one figure only sold at a gas station in rural Nevada for 12 minutes in 1996. It's not just about owning things. Many of these collectibles have deep lore and worldb building from the mysterious backstories of Transformers to the lore in the card text on Pokemon cards. That's just plain ridiculous. Collecting is sort of like role-playing a historian. But then ask yourself is there truly an end? Collecting can possibly turn into hoarding if left unchecked. The anterior singulate cortex which helps us let go of things can be weakened over time if the reward system part of your brain is overactive. It's all about balance. As long as your love of collecting things isn't hurting you or anyone around you go for it. And honestly for a lot of people collecting is also about value. Some people choose stocks. Other people choose Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle toys from the 80s and '90s. Research shows that rare comics cards and toys have historically earned real returns over time. But here's the very big catch. Condition is everything. You should know what you're doing before you dive deep into this hobby. And that's where today's sponsor CGA comes in. CGA or the Collectible Grading Authority is the trusted name in grading and authenticating collectible toys and video games. They're the gold standard for serious and casual collectors alike. They've graded hundreds of thousands of vintage action figures and video games using strict standards that collectors have relied on for over two decades. Whether it's from the 1980s or last year's Comic-Con exclusive CGA helps preserve value and protect against fakes. And because collectibles don't have a stock exchange or price tag that lasts forever CGA's grading creates a universal benchmark. It's how top collectors auction houses and dealers agree on what's truly mint. And if you're just starting out CGA is an awesome way to learn the ropes and avoid getting scammed by someone trying to sell you a super rare Sonic the Hedgehog that's actually just blue Play-Doh in a sock. If you've got something cool sitting in a box or a whole collection you've been building since the '90s CGA is a great place to start if you want to protect sell or simply showcase your collectibles like a pro. ""Even though it’s something that happens to  all of us humans don’t like talking about   death. I get it. This channel IS called  LIFE Noggin after all. People don’t want   to keep on thinking about death. But how we  honor the recently departed can get REALLY   interesting! From mourning to celebrating  or even launching loved ones into space    we can learn a lot from how we treat our  dead! Think of this episode as a memento   mori. It might make you appreciate life  AND rethink that boring old headstone idea! Welcome to Life Noggin: Big Brain a deeper dive  into topics you and your noggin might care about!   This is a new thing we’re trying out so let  us know what you think of these Big Brains! All over the world people have different  ways of honoring the dead. Some of the   most common include burial as seen  in Judaism Islam and Christianity    where the body is placed in the ground  with specific religious rituals. Others   choose cremation especially in Hinduism and  Buddhism where the body is burned to release   the soul and begin its next journey. Some are  celebrations like Día de los Muertos in Mexico    where families decorate altars and throw parties  to welcome back the spirits of their loved ones. Most of you have probably heard of these so  let’s get into the ones you probably haven’t. First up is the sky burial. In parts of  Tibet and Mongolia the body is taken   to a mountaintop and left for vultures. It  might sound brutal but it’s actually rooted   in compassion. Buddhist teachings hold that once  the soul has moved on the body is just an empty   vessel. Rather than letting it rot or be sealed  away sky burial offers the body back to nature    feeding other living things in the process.  And since the frozen rocky terrain of the   Himalayans makes traditional burial nearly  impossible it's actually pretty practical!   Leave me on top of BlockRock Mountain and let  the mouse pointers peck at my pixel coating. Over in Madagascar families take part in a  tradition called Famadihana or the Turning of the   Bones. Every few years relatives gather to reopen  the family tomb gently remove the remains of   their ancestors and carefully rewrap the bones in  fresh cloth usually silk. The wrapped remains are   then carried above the crowd often while dancing  to live music. People share food tell stories    and sometimes even spray the bundles with perfume  or take photos with them. Once the celebration is   over the bodies are returned to the tomb until  the next gathering. It’s a hands-on ritual that   keeps the memory of the dead alive and shows  that even in death family is never forgotten.
